say.en: Sorting 10 marks takes no time. Sorting the marks of all ten lakh students who take the board exam is a different story. Time complexity tells us how the work grows with the size of the data. In this lesson: Estimate time complexity from loops.
Explain why the three sorts are n squared.
Predict how time grows when n doubles.

body.en: The time an algorithm takes depends on how many instructions run as the input size n grows. Simple rules: an algorithm with no loop has constant *time complexity*, 1; one loop from 1 to n has complexity n; a loop within a loop has complexity n²; if there is a nested loop and also a single loop, the nested loop decides it, n².

title.en: On the board: Counting loops to find time complexity

say.en: Count how the number of steps grows with the input size n. Code with no loop takes the same time for any n: constant.
One loop from 1 to n runs n times: linear.
A loop inside a loop runs n times n: quadratic. Bubble, selection and insertion sort all have nested loops.
On a graph, n squared shoots up much faster than n. Doubling n doubles a linear algorithm’s time but makes a quadratic one four times slower.

body.en: Bubble, selection and insertion sort each use a nested loop over the list, so all three have time *complexity* n². For example, bubble sort without an early stop makes (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, which grows like n². Doubling n makes such an algorithm about four times slower.
